semester.title: Semester I
semester.name: Foundations of Human Behavior, Evidence & Executive Leadership

description: Semester I, *Foundations of Human Behavior, Evidence & Executive Leadership*, is a 14-week program in how people judge, decide, learn, lead and negotiate, and how organizations turn evidence, strategy, finance and law into decisions. It moves from the individual (judgment, motivation, learning, evidence) to the social (leadership, power, negotiation) and the organizational (design, strategy, finance, law, execution, ethics), and ends in an executive capstone that uses all of it.

The course draws on 3 schools — School of Behavioral & Social Science, School of Business & Leadership, School of Law & Strategy — and on a research library of 197 verified sources. It is written for working professionals and asks for about 5–7 hours a week.

philosophy.title: Evidence, labelled
philosophy.text: Every passage of every lesson says what it is — established research, a contested finding, APERTURE’s own explanation, an illustrative example, a professional application or a speculative hypothesis — and research claims cite the library.

philosophy.title: Mastery before momentum
philosophy.text: Quizzes and the midterm set mastery at 80%. Below it, you get the lessons and concepts behind your misses and a reassessment drawn from reserve questions.

philosophy.title: Retrieval and spacing
philosophy.text: Comprehension checks after each lesson, 220 spaced-repetition review cards and weekly reflections turn reading into memory.

philosophy.title: Calibration over confidence
philosophy.text: Labs and assessments ask how sure you are, not only what you think, so the semester measures the match between confidence and accuracy.

philosophy.title: Practice on realistic problems
philosophy.text: Each week pairs an interactive lab with an original case (15 in all) and an applied assignment written as professional work.

philosophy.title: Honest assessment
philosophy.text: Objective items are auto-graded with the scoring rules shown on every results page. Written work is self-assessed against published rubrics and labelled as such; automated checks cover format only, never content.

formats.title: Written lessons

formats.title: Readings

formats.title: Interactive labs

formats.title: Cases

formats.title: Assessments
formats.text: A weekly quiz (162 questions), a weekly applied assignment, a midterm after Week 7 and the executive capstone. A baseline diagnostic in Week 1 is not graded.

organization.name: Port Calder Lamplighters (fictional)
organization.context: A fictional mid-market club in the fictional 30-club Meridian League. Payroll sits in the league’s lower-middle third; the club finished 79–83 last season, four games out of the final postseason place. It operates a minor-league system of five affiliates and an international academy, and has just created a Department of Advance and Strategic Coordination. All people, organizations, figures and events are invented.

capstone.fiction: All people, organizations, leagues and data in this capstone are fictional and synthetic. The Port Calder Lamplighters and the Meridian League are invented; nothing describes or is modeled on any real club’s internal structure. Legal points are educational and general — not legal advice.

deliverables.title: Strategic memorandum
deliverables.description: The comprehensive strategy addressed to the president and GM: recommendation first, then diagnosis, mission, priorities, technology, stakeholders, legal and ethical issues, communication, evidence standards and risks, with structure, budget and roadmap summarized and referenced. Assembling it from the components requires cutting: integrate, do not staple. Self-assessed against this rubric.

deliverables.title: Executive summary
deliverables.description: A one-page summary that the president could forward to ownership unchanged: recommendation, why, cost, first-year milestones, top risks and the decisions requested. Self-assessed against this rubric.

deliverables.title: Organizational chart
deliverables.description: The chart built in the Organization Builder with a narrative explaining structure, staffing and decision rights, the Builder checks you pass and those you accept failing, and why. Self-assessed against this rubric; the Builder’s checks are automated and transparent.

deliverables.title: Budget model
deliverables.description: A Year 1 budget with a three-year view: personnel envelope, operating line and the investment portfolio from the Capital Allocation Lab, with NPV results, scenario tests and a narrative explaining departures from the NPV ranking. Self-assessed against this rubric; the lab’s calculations are automated.

deliverables.title: Implementation roadmap
deliverables.description: The first 90 days, change approach, indicators and the gated three-year roadmap in one document, with owners, dependencies, signals and decision gates. Self-assessed against this rubric.

deliverables.title: Decision presentation
deliverables.description: Ten to twelve slides with speaker notes, drafted in the Executive Communication Studio, plus the written defense of major decisions prepared for the president’s questions. Self-assessed against this rubric; the Studio’s text metrics are automated.

deliverables.title: Reflection on strengths and areas for development
deliverables.description: A private reflection, drawing on your capstone work, your learning profile and your Decision Journal, on what you demonstrated and where you need to develop. Self-assessed; research reviews find self-assessment only modestly accurate ([Dunning, Heath and Suls 2004](R-dunning-2004-flawed)), so anchor every claim to evidence from your own work.

ai: APERTURE’s original explanations, cases, quiz items, lecture scripts and this syllabus were drafted with AI assistance and are labelled as APERTURE material, not research. Research claims are tied to library records whose bibliographic details were checked; the library records how each was verified.
Lecture narration is synthesized speech (the open Kokoro-82M voice model). It reads APERTURE’s scripts; it is not a recording of a person.
The optional ChatGPT study prompts are a study aid. Graded written work — assignments, short answers and capstone deliverables — should be your own; you assess it yourself against the rubric.
integrity.fiction: All people, organizations and data in cases, exercises, the midterm and the capstone are fictional and say so. Legal material is educational and general, never legal advice.

gaps.detail: Semester I is self-paced. The curriculum has no start date, due dates or session times, so the schedule is given by week number only.
APERTURE is self-directed. There is no instructor, teaching staff, office hours or discussion section.
V1 reports a weighted percentage standing over completed components. It defines no letter-grade scale, passing mark, honors or failing grade, and awards no credit.
V1 sets no limit on quiz or midterm attempts, no deadlines and no late penalties. A reassessment becomes available after an attempt below mastery.

The curriculum stores week-level objectives, not a course description, philosophy or semester outcomes. Those sections of this syllabus are composed from the weekly objectives and the application’s own features.
The stated workload is 5–7 hours a week. The planned hours of Week 4 (7.45 h) and Week 13 (7.3 h) are slightly above 7.
Library metadata was verified through search results; 197 of 197 links are marked “link untested” until opened in a browser, and 27 records are only partially confirmed.
5 of 60 narrated lectures are released. The other 55 are scripted and marked Coming Soon; every lesson is complete in its written form.
